![](images/51/517c8b69f022d892daa4f8f48a74f6a93b12143e71f5077a046133b1b396ee9f.svg)" :question/worked-solution "To find a basis of $\textrm{Null}(A),$ we need to solve the equation $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ and express the solution as a linear combination of linearly independent vectors. Those vectors form a basis of $\textrm{Null}(A).$

Since $A\sim B,$ the equation $A \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ is equivalent to the equation $B\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0},$ which corresponds to the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{2}-\frac{1}{3}{x}_{3}+\frac{2}{3}{x}_{4}=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the general solution is $x_1=0$ and $x_2=\dfrac{1}{3}x_3 - \dfrac{2}{3} x_4$ where $x_3$ and $x_4$ are free variables. Therefore, if $\mathbf{x}\in\textrm{Null}(A),$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{4}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ \frac{1}{3}{x}_{3}-\frac{2}{3}{x}_{4} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{4}\end{aligned}]={x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ \frac{1}{3} \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{4}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -\frac{2}{3} \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3},{x}_{4}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

This implies that

![](images/50/50bf947d3beddfb5be8eee27c0d77bf57f3e93204a8554ffffa1e4cc41f35956.svg)

is a basis of $\textrm{Null}(A)$ since it is a linearly independent set and its vectors generate $\textrm{Null}(A).$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186119819 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-bf0f365d-7946-58fa-b12c-812741af29fb"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186119630 :question/problem "Given the matrix ![](images/ec/ec919391ecd75553fc12f04d1cb6832c7019677ff0954eaffded42fd2cdb8cc2.svg) find a basis of $\textrm{Null}(A).$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-042d970d-9326-52e7-be56-f67cc5dc1c6c" :question/id #uuid "042d970d-9326-52e7-be56-f67cc5dc1c6c" :question/math-academy-id "q-111295" :question/problem "Given that  $\text{Null}(A)={[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{3} \\ -{x}_{3} \\ 4{x}_{3}\end{aligned}]\,:\,{x}_{3}\in R}$, find a basis for $\text{Null}(A).$" :question/worked-solution "Any vector in $\text{Null}(A)$ has the form

$$
[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{3} \\ -{x}_{3} \\ 4{x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Expanding, we get

$$
[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{3} \\ -{x}_{3} \\ 4{x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, a basis for $\text{Null}(A)$ is

$$
B={[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]}
$$

since it is a linearly independent set and its vectors generate $\text{Null}(A).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields 17592186121041 :tutorial/content "Remember that the null space $\textrm{Null}(A)$ of a matrix $A$ consists of the solutions to the equation $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}.$ To find a basis of $\textrm{Null}(A),$ we solve the equation $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ and express the solution as a linear combination of linearly independent vectors. Those vectors form a basis of $\textrm{Null}(A).$

To illustrate, consider the matrix ![](images/70/702794c0129df672cc7c4cc65260c9bfa7e33804ea9f71bba048cf62142a0a18.svg) Computing the reduced row echelon form of $A,$ we get

![](images/16/16d52c068c616e2eca149a8e81929a98c85726361d7ea2291ab314fe7567e4ce.svg)

So, the equation $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ is equivalent to the system

![](images/bb/bb8743bd8eb072476af0e9e31c0215916beeeb82fc371348de1e6013b38810f8.svg)

where $\color{blue}x_1$ and $\color{blue}x_2$ are basic variables (corresponding to the pivot columns) and $\color{red}x_3$ is a free variable (corresponding to the non-pivot column).

Therefore, any vector $\mathbf{x}$ in $\textrm{Null}(A)$ has the form

![](images/6e/6e124e2c030f6cad72932d09211935b438f1189322ded40683a1f18618e35f3e.svg)

So, the set ![](images/24/2449d6abf866e2baa123e81c1d610940930c75c6b45ecf818d36c62191ef605f.svg) is a basis of $\textrm{Null}(A)$ since it is a linearly independent set and the vector $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ generates the null space of $A.$

**Note:** It might be the case that $\textrm{Null}(A)$ for a particular matrix $A$ equals the so-called zero subspace $\{ \mathbf{0} \}$ containing only the zero-vector. The basis of $\{ \mathbf{0} \}$ is said to be the *empty set*, which is a set that does not contain any vectors. 17592186121041 :tutorial/content "Remember that the null space $\textrm{Null}(A)$ of a matrix $A$ consists of the solutions to the equation $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}.$ To find a basis of Those vectors form a basis of $\textrm{Null}(A).$

To illustrate, consider the matrix ![](images/70/702794c0129df672cc7c4cc65260c9bfa7e33804ea9f71bba048cf62142a0a18.svg) Computing the reduced row echelon form of $A,$ we get

![](images/16/16d52c068c616e2eca149a8e81929a98c85726361d7ea2291ab314fe7567e4ce.svg)

So, the equation $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ is equivalent to the system

![](images/bb/bb8743bd8eb072476af0e9e31c0215916beeeb82fc371348de1e6013b38810f8.svg)

where $\color{blue}x_1$ and $\color{blue}x_2$ are basic variables (corresponding to the pivot columns) and $\color{red}x_3$ is a free variable (corresponding to the non-pivot column).

Therefore, any vector $\mathbf{x}$ in $\textrm{Null}(A)$ has the form

![](images/6e/6e124e2c030f6cad72932d09211935b438f1189322ded40683a1f18618e35f3e.svg)

So, the set ![](images/24/2449d6abf866e2baa123e81c1d610940930c75c6b45ecf818d36c62191ef605f.svg) is a basis of $\textrm{Null}(A)$ since it is a linearly independent set and the vector $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ generates the null space of $A.$

$$

$$

$$

Since $A\sim B,$ the equation $A \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ is equivalent to the equation $B\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0},$ which corresponds to the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{2}-\frac{1}{3}{x}_{3}+\frac{2}{3}{x}_{4}=0\end{aligned}
$$
